notes.front: What is a Cloud Billing account?
notes.back: The account that defines who pays for a set of Google Cloud resources and tracks all costs from the projects linked to it.
notes.explanation: It tracks both charges and savings, for every project linked to it.
notes.example: Like a company credit-card account that several departments’ projects charge to, with one statement for all of them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Billing overview”, “Cloud Billing accounts”
notes.evidence: A Cloud Billing account is set up in Google Cloud and defines who pays for a given set of Google Cloud resources and Google Maps Platform APIs. This account is used to track all of the costs (charges and savings) incurred by your Google Cloud usage in all projects linked to the Cloud Billing account.

notes.front: What is a budget alert in Cloud Billing?
notes.back: An email sent when actual or forecasted costs exceed a percentage of a budget, according to threshold rules you set.
notes.explanation: Threshold rules are what trigger these emails; the recipients are ones you specify.
notes.example: Like a bank texting you when your monthly card spending passes 90% of the limit you chose, except it only warns you.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: You can set threshold rules to trigger email alert notifications. When your actual costs or forecasted costs exceed a percentage of your budget (based on the rules you set), alert emails are sent to the recipients you specify.

notes.front: What is a label on a Google Cloud resource?
notes.back: A key-value pair you assign to a resource to organise resources and manage costs.
notes.explanation: Label information is forwarded to the billing system, so you can break down billed charges by label.
notes.example: Like writing “team: payroll” on a storage box so you can later count every box that belongs to payroll.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Resource Manager: Labels overview”, “What are labels?”
notes.evidence: A label is a key-value pair that you can assign to Google Cloud resources. They help you organize these resources and manage your costs at scale, with the granularity you need.

notes.front: What is a committed use discount (CUD)?
notes.back: A discount received for buying a commitment to a minimum amount of resource usage or spend for one or three years.
notes.explanation: For Compute Engine, the commitment earns deeply discounted prices for virtual machine instances.
notes.example: Like a mobile phone contract: you agree to pay for a set amount each month for a fixed term, and get a lower rate in return.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud offers CUDs in return for purchasing committed use contracts (also known as commitments). When you purchase a commitment, you commit either to a minimum amount of resource usage or to a minimum spend amount for a specified term duration of one or three years.

notes.front: What is a sustained use discount (SUD)?
notes.back: A Compute Engine discount on resources used for more than 25% of a billing month that receive no other discount.
notes.explanation: The discount grows with each further hour of use, up to 20% or 30% for a full month depending on machine type; only the machine series Google lists qualify.
notes.example: Like a gym that lowers each extra visit’s price once you have come on more than a quarter of the month’s days, without a contract.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Sustained use discounts”, “Sustained use discounts”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine offers sustained use discounts (SUDs) on resources that are used for more than 25% of a billing month and are not receiving any other discounts.

notes.front: What is Active Assist?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s portfolio of tools that generate recommendations and insights to help you optimise your projects.
notes.explanation: It includes recommenders, which generate recommendations and insights, and analysis tools.
notes.example: Like a building inspector who walks your estate and leaves notes on idle rooms and unlocked doors, but leaves the decision to you.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Active Assist”, “What is Active Assist”
notes.evidence: Active Assist refers to the portfolio of tools used in Google Cloud to generate recommendations and insights to help you optimize your Google Cloud projects.

notes.front: What is a quota in Google Cloud?
notes.back: A restriction on how much of a Google Cloud resource your project can use.
notes.explanation: Quotas help ensure fairness and reduce spikes in resource use, and protect the community of users from overloaded services.
notes.example: Like a library allowing each member ten books at a time: the limit is per member, and you can ask for more.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Cloud Quotas overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud uses quotas to help ensure fairness and reduce spikes in resource use and availability. A quota restricts how much of a Google Cloud resource your Google Cloud project can use.

notes.front: Do the Well-Architected Framework’s pillars address functional or non-functional requirements?
notes.back: Non-functional ones: each pillar covers a non-functional focus area such as security, reliability, performance or cost.
notes.explanation: The six focus areas are security, reliability, performance, cost, operations and sustainability.
notes.contrast: A feature the system offers to its users is not one of these focus areas.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Well-Architected Framework pillars and perspectives”
notes.evidence: A pillar in the Well-Architected Framework provides principles and recommendations for a specific non-functional focus area: security, reliability, performance, cost, operations, or sustainability.

notes.front: Which of these requirements for a ticket-booking app falls within one of the framework’s non-functional focus areas?
notes.back: A: Keep serving bookings if a whole zone fails.
notes.choices:
A) Keep serving bookings if a whole zone fails
B) Email each customer a ticket after payment
C) Let customers choose a seat on a seating plan
D) Let staff refund a cancelled booking
notes.choicesExplained: C, B and D each describe something the app does for a user; none is about security, reliability, performance, cost, operations or sustainability.
notes.explanation: Staying available through failures belongs to reliability, one of the six non-functional focus areas.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework”, “Pillars”
notes.evidence: Reliability Design and operate resilient and highly available workloads in the cloud.

notes.front: Which four workload disposition strategies does the Professional Cloud Architect exam guide give as examples?
notes.back: Build, buy, modify and deprecate.
notes.explanation: The guide lists them under the business requirements an architect weighs when designing a solution.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Professional Cloud Architect exam guide”, “Section 1.1”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: An old in-house fax-to-email tool has had no users for a year, and nobody will migrate it. Which of the exam guide’s disposition strategies fits it?
notes.back: D: Deprecate.
notes.choices:
A) Modify
B) Build
C) Buy
D) Deprecate
notes.choicesExplained: B and C would create or acquire a replacement nobody needs. A would spend effort changing a tool that has no users.
notes.explanation: A workload that no one needs is retired rather than rebuilt, bought or changed.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Professional Cloud Architect exam guide”, “Section 1.1”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: Which two success measurements does the exam guide give as examples, besides metrics in general?
notes.back: Key performance indicators and return on investment.
notes.explanation: The guide groups them as ways to measure whether a solution succeeds for the business.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Professional Cloud Architect exam guide”, “Section 1.1”
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: How does the cost pillar contrast on-premises and cloud cost models?
notes.back: On-premises costs include capital and operational expenditure; most cloud resource costs are operational expenditure, incurred when consumed.
notes.explanation: On-premises assets are bought and their cost depreciated over their operating life.
notes.contrast: Cloud: pay as resources are consumed, rather than buying assets up front.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: On-premises IT costs include capital expenditure (CapEx) and operational expenditure (OpEx). On-premises hardware and software assets are acquired and the acquisition costs are depreciated over the operating life of the assets. In the cloud, the costs for most cloud resources are treated as OpEx, where costs are incurred when the cloud resources are consumed.

notes.front: A finance director expects the move to Google Cloud to replace a large hardware purchase every five years with charges that follow actual use. Which cost model is she describing for the cloud?
notes.back: D: Operational expenditure, incurred as resources are consumed.
notes.choices:
A) Capital expenditure, depreciated over the assets’ life
B) Capital expenditure, paid at contract signature
C) A mix in which hardware stays capital expenditure
D) Operational expenditure, incurred as resources are consumed
notes.choicesExplained: A describes the on-premises model of buying and depreciating assets. B and C keep an up-front asset purchase, which consumption-based cloud charges replace.
notes.explanation: The cost pillar says most cloud resource costs are treated as operational expenditure, incurred on consumption.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”, “Well-Architected Framework: Cost optimization pillar”
notes.evidence: In the cloud, the costs for most cloud resources are treated as OpEx, where costs are incurred when the cloud resources are consumed.

notes.front: How does a Cloud Billing account differ from a Google payments profile?
notes.back: The billing account is a cloud-level resource in the Google Cloud console; the payments profile is Google-level, in the Google payments center.
notes.explanation: The payments profile connects to all your Google services and stores payment instruments.
notes.contrast: Payments profile: shared across Google services, not only Google Cloud.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Billing overview”, “Cloud Billing accounts”
notes.evidence: A Google payments profile: Is a Google-level resource managed in the Google payments center.

notes.front: What are the two types of Cloud Billing account, and how is each paid?
notes.back: Self-serve (online): credit or debit card or direct debit. Invoiced (offline): cheque or wire transfer, with invoices.
notes.explanation: You can sign up for a self-serve account online, but you must be eligible for invoiced billing.
notes.contrast: Only the invoiced type requires eligibility.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Billing overview”, “Cloud Billing account types”
notes.evidence: Invoiced (or Offline) account The billable status of an invoiced account is Paid account. Payment instrument can be check or wire transfer.

notes.front: Three product teams each run their own projects, but finance wants a single place that tracks the charges and savings of all of them. What should the projects share?
notes.back: A: One Cloud Billing account linked to all three projects.
notes.choices:
A) One Cloud Billing account linked to all three projects
B) One label on every resource
C) One quota for all three projects
D) One budget alert per project
notes.choicesExplained: B helps break costs down but does not make one account pay and track them. C restricts usage and does not track costs. D warns about spending but does not decide who pays.
notes.explanation: A Cloud Billing account tracks all costs, charges and savings, of every project linked to it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Billing overview”, “Cloud Billing accounts”
notes.evidence: This account is used to track all of the costs (charges and savings) incurred by your Google Cloud usage in all projects linked to the Cloud Billing account.

notes.front: When you first create a budget, the default alert thresholds are {{c1::50%, 90% and 100%}} of the budget amount, against actual spend.
notes.explanation: You can change the percentages, the type of spend, and add or remove threshold rules.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Alert threshold rules”
notes.evidence: When you first create a budget, the default alert thresholds are set at 50%, 90%, and 100% of the budget amount, calculated against Actual spend.

notes.front: What are two levels at which a Cloud Billing budget can apply?
notes.back: Any two of: a whole Cloud Billing account; organisations, folders or projects; services; resources with a specific label.
notes.explanation: Scoping a budget narrows which costs it tracks.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Your budget can apply at any of these levels: An entire Cloud Billing account. One or more organizations, folders, or projects that are associated with your Cloud Billing account. One or more services, such as Compute Engine or BigQuery. Resources that have a specific label applied to them.

notes.front: Does an alerts-only budget stop usage or spending when it is exceeded?
notes.back: No. It only triggers alerts; it does not automatically cap usage or spending.
notes.explanation: Budget alert emails might prompt you to act, but they do not prevent use or billing of services.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”
notes.evidence: Setting an alerts-only budget doesn't automatically cap Google Cloud or Google Maps Platform usage or spending.

notes.front: Which messaging service do budgets use for programmatic notifications, for example to disable billing on a project that exceeds its budget?
notes.back: Pub/Sub.
notes.explanation: Programmatic notifications can trigger actions and automate cost management tasks.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Programmatic notifications”
notes.evidence: You can use programmatic notifications to trigger an action, such as forwarding your budget messages to other mediums (for example, Slack), and to automate cost management tasks (such as disabling billing on a project when it exceeds its budget amount). You use Pub/Sub notifications to programmatically receive spend updates about this budget.

notes.front: A research group’s sandbox project must stop incurring charges automatically once it passes its monthly budget, even at night. What should the architect set up?
notes.back: A: A budget with programmatic notifications through Pub/Sub that trigger disabling billing on the project.
notes.choices:
A) A budget with programmatic notifications through Pub/Sub that trigger disabling billing on the project
B) An alerts-only budget with a 100% threshold rule
C) Extra email recipients on the budget alert
D) A lower quota on the project
notes.choicesExplained: B and C only send alerts, which do not stop use or billing. D limits some resource usage but is not tied to the budget amount.
notes.explanation: Alerts-only budgets never cap spending, but programmatic notifications can automate tasks such as disabling billing. A spend cap budget, in preview for some services, is a newer option.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Programmatic notifications”
notes.evidence: You can use programmatic notifications to trigger an action, such as forwarding your budget messages to other mediums (for example, Slack), and to automate cost management tasks (such as disabling billing on a project when it exceeds its budget amount).

notes.front: A manager wants an email as soon as the month’s spending is projected to pass the budget, rather than after it has done so. How should the threshold rule be set?
notes.back: C: Trigger on forecasted spend.
notes.choices:
A) Remove all threshold rules
B) Trigger on actual spend at 100%
C) Trigger on forecasted spend
D) Switch the budget to a yearly period
notes.choicesExplained: B fires only once costs have accrued. A stops email alerts altogether. D changes the tracking period, not when the alert fires.
notes.explanation: Thresholds can be set for forecasted costs, estimated out to the end of the budget period, instead of costs already accrued.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Create, edit, or delete budgets and budget alerts”, “Alert threshold rules”
notes.evidence: Thresholds can be set for actual costs accrued during the budget period, or for forecasted costs (estimated costs calculated out to the end of the current calendar budget period).

notes.front: How can labels help you find the cost of, say, all test resources versus production ones?
notes.back: Export billing data to BigQuery: labels are exported with the resources and their usage, so you can query costs by label.
notes.explanation: Labels are also forwarded to the billing system, so built-in reports can filter and group costs by label.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Resource Manager: Labels overview”, “Understand costs using labels”
notes.evidence: You can enable the export of billing data to BigQuery. Labels are exported to BigQuery with the corresponding Google Cloud resources and their usage.

notes.front: Labels and tags can both be attached to resources. Which one can set conditions on policies?
notes.back: Tags. Labels are queryable annotations but cannot be used to set conditions on policies.
notes.explanation: Tags can conditionally allow or deny policies depending on whether a resource carries them.
notes.contrast: Labels: for organising resources and breaking down costs.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Resource Manager: Labels overview”, “Labels and tags”
notes.evidence: Labels can be used as queryable annotations for resources, but can't be used to set conditions on policies. Tags provide a way to conditionally allow or deny policies based on whether a resource has a specific tag

notes.front: A company wants a monthly report of cloud costs per cost centre, where resources from several cost centres share the same projects. What should it do?
notes.back: C: Apply cost-centre labels to resources and filter or group billing costs by label.
notes.choices:
A) Create a separate Cloud Billing account per cost centre
B) Set a quota per cost centre
C) Apply cost-centre labels to resources and filter or group billing costs by label
D) Use tags to set policy conditions per cost centre
notes.choicesExplained: A works per project, and these cost centres share projects. B limits usage but reports no costs. D is for conditionally allowing or denying policies, not for breaking down costs.
notes.explanation: Label information reaches the billing system, so charges can be broken down by label even inside one project.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Resource Manager: Labels overview”, “Understand costs using labels”
notes.evidence: You can add labels such as costcenter=cost_center_name, service=service_name, and environment=environment_name to your VMs or Cloud Storage buckets. This allows you to understand where your resources are deployed, for what purpose, and the cost center to which they should be charged.

notes.front: What does a resource-based commitment commit you to, and what usage is it ideal for?
notes.back: A minimum amount of Compute Engine resources in a specific region and machine configuration; ideal for predictable, steady-state usage.
notes.explanation: The commitment is linked to the region in which you buy it, and covers resources only there.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Resource-based CUDs”
notes.evidence: Resource-based commitments are ideal for predictable and steady state usage. These commitments provide a discount in exchange for your commitment to purchase a minimum amount of Compute Engine resources.

notes.front: What does a compute flexible commitment commit you to, and across which services does it give discounts?
notes.back: A minimum amount of hourly spend; discounts apply across Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine and Cloud Run.
notes.explanation: For Compute Engine it removes the need to tie the commitment to one project, region or machine configuration.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Compute flexible CUDs”
notes.evidence: Compute flexible CUDs add flexibility to your Google Cloud spending capabilities by providing discounts for your spend across Compute Engine, GKE, and Cloud Run. Specifically for Compute Engine, compute flexible CUDs eliminate the need to restrict your commitments to a single project, region, or machine configuration.

notes.front: Can you cancel a resource-based commitment once bought, and are you billed if you do not use the resources?
notes.back: No, it cannot be cancelled; you are billed monthly until the term ends, whether or not you use the resources.
notes.explanation: Resource-based commitments are described as ideal for predictable, steady-state usage.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Resource-based CUDs”
notes.evidence: You are billed monthly for your committed resources until the end of your commitment term, regardless of whether or not you use those resources. You can't cancel a commitment after its purchase.

notes.front: Can two kinds of discount apply to the same portion of Compute Engine usage?
notes.back: No. Discount types are mutually exclusive; a resource is eligible for only one kind at a time.
notes.explanation: When both commitment types exist, resource-based commitments are applied first each hour.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Order of discount application”
notes.evidence: However, the discount types that Google Cloud offers on your Compute Engine resources are mutually exclusive and can't be combined. At any given point, a resource is eligible for only one kind of discount.

notes.front: A company’s compute use is steady in total but moves between regions and machine types, and some runs on Cloud Run. Which commitment fits best?
notes.back: C: A compute flexible commitment.
notes.choices:
A) A resource-based commitment in one region
B) A resource-based commitment for each machine type
C) A compute flexible commitment
D) No commitment; rely on sustained use discounts
notes.choicesExplained: A and B cover only the region and machine configuration they name, which this usage keeps changing. D applies only to Compute Engine and Google Kubernetes Engine virtual machines, so Cloud Run spend would get none.
notes.explanation: Compute flexible commitments are not tied to one project, region or machine configuration and cover Compute Engine and Cloud Run spend.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Committed use discounts (CUDs) for Compute Engine”, “Order of discount application”
notes.evidence: You can use compute flexible commitments to cover any resource usage that isn't specific to any one region, project, or machine configuration.

notes.front: What must you do to receive sustained use discounts?
notes.back: Nothing: Compute Engine calculates and applies them automatically within a Cloud Billing account.
notes.explanation: You receive them as monthly credits for eligible resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Sustained use discounts”, “How sustained use discounts work”
notes.evidence: Compute Engine automatically calculates and applies SUDs to resource usage within a Cloud Billing account, so there is no action required on your part to enable these discounts.

notes.front: Do sustained use discounts apply to usage already covered by committed use discounts?
notes.back: No. Sustained use discounts do not apply to usage covered by CUDs.
notes.explanation: The limitations also say only self-serve (online) Cloud Billing accounts are eligible.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Sustained use discounts”, “Sustained use discounts”
notes.evidence: Only Self-serve (or Online) Cloud Billing accounts are eligible for receiving SUDs. SUDs don't apply to the resource usage that is already covered by committed use discounts (CUDs).

notes.front: A team runs a Compute Engine instance from a machine series eligible for sustained use discounts for the whole month, with no commitment, on a self-serve billing account. What discount does it get, and how?
notes.back: A: A sustained use discount, applied automatically, that grows with use through the month.
notes.choices:
A) A sustained use discount, applied automatically, that grows with use through the month
B) None, because it bought no commitment
C) A committed use discount, once the team requests it
D) A sustained use discount, after the team enables it for the project
notes.choicesExplained: B ignores sustained use discounts, which need no commitment. C needs a purchased commitment. D is wrong because no action is needed to enable sustained use discounts.
notes.explanation: Use beyond a quarter of the month earns a growing discount with no action needed, up to 20% or 30% for a full month depending on machine type.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Sustained use discounts”, “Sustained use discounts”
notes.evidence: The discount increases incrementally with usage and you can get up to a 30% net discount off of the resource cost for virtual machine (VM) instances that run the entire month.

notes.front: Into how many value categories do recommenders’ recommendations fall?
notes.back: Six.
notes.explanation: The categories help you optimise your cloud in a variety of ways.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Active Assist”, “Recommenders and Recommendations”
notes.evidence: Recommenders generate recommendations that fall into six value categories that can help you optimize your cloud in a variety of ways.

notes.front: What does Google advise before you apply Active Assist recommendations?
notes.back: Have a reviewer in your organisation assess their impacts; if you apply them without human review, set up a rollback process first.
notes.explanation: Unassessed changes could hurt performance or reliability, or remove required permissions.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Active Assist”, “Apply recommendations”
notes.evidence: Before applying recommendations in the Google Cloud console or using the API, ensure that impacts are assessed by a reviewer within your organization.

notes.front: An architect wants a list of idle or oversized resources across projects, with suggested changes she can review and then apply or dismiss. What should she use?
notes.back: D: Active Assist recommendations.
notes.choices:
A) Lower quotas
B) A budget alert
C) Labels on every resource
D) Active Assist recommendations
notes.choicesExplained: B warns about spending but suggests no changes. C lets you break down costs but finds nothing idle. A restricts usage without identifying what to change.
notes.explanation: Active Assist generates recommendations and insights, and lets you apply or dismiss them.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “What is Active Assist”, “Manage recommendations and insights”
notes.evidence: In Active Assist, you can choose to apply or dismiss the recommendations. Some recommendations can be applied automatically, while other recommendations require additional steps to complete.

notes.front: Which type of quota restricts how much of a resource Google Cloud allocates to you, such as the number of virtual machines in a project?
notes.back: Allocation quota.
notes.explanation: It is one of three quota types, with rate and concurrent quotas.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Types of quotas”
notes.evidence: Allocation quotas: Allocation quotas restrict how much of a resource Google Cloud allocates to you. For example, Compute Engine applies an allocation quota to the number of VMs allocated for a Google Cloud project.

notes.front: Which type of quota restricts how much of a resource you may consume over a stated time period?
notes.back: Rate quota.
notes.explanation: A rate quota specifies both the time period and the amount allowed within it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Types of quotas”
notes.evidence: Rate quotas: Rate quotas restrict the rate at which you can consume a resource. Rate quotas specify a time period, and the amount of the resource that you are permitted to consume over that time period.

notes.front: Which type of quota restricts the number of operations running at the same time, usually long-running ones?
notes.back: Concurrent quota.
notes.explanation: Some Compute Engine insert operations, which can run for up to an hour, are limited this way.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Types of quotas”
notes.evidence: Concurrent quotas: Concurrent quotas restrict the number of operations that run concurrently. Concurrent quotas usually apply to long-running operations.

notes.front: How does a quota differ from a system limit?
notes.back: A quota value can be adjusted on request; a system limit is a fixed constraint, such as a maximum file size, that cannot be changed.
notes.explanation: Many services have both.
notes.contrast: Quota: request an adjustment. System limit: design around it.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Cloud Quotas overview”
notes.evidence: Many services also have system limits. System limits are fixed constraints, such as maximum file sizes or database schema limitations, which cannot be increased or decreased.

notes.front: Who evaluates most quota adjustment requests?
notes.back: Automated systems, based on criteria such as resource availability and how long you have used Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: Some requests are escalated to human reviewers, and for increases you might be asked to pay in advance.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “About quota adjustments”
notes.evidence: Most quota adjustment requests are evaluated by automated systems. Their decision is based on criteria including the availability of resources, the length of time you've used Google Cloud, and other factors.

notes.front: A project hits an error because a Google Cloud service allows it only 600 calls per minute, and the error clears a minute later. Which quota type was reached?
notes.back: C: A rate quota.
notes.choices:
A) An allocation quota
B) A concurrent quota
C) A rate quota
D) A system limit
notes.choicesExplained: A limits how much is allocated, such as a count of machines, and does not reset each minute. B limits operations running at once. D is fixed and does not clear with time.
notes.explanation: Rate quotas limit consumption over a time period, and available quota resets when the period resets.
notes.source: Google Cloud, “Cloud Quotas overview”, “Types of quotas”
notes.evidence: Rate quotas: Rate quotas restrict the rate at which you can consume a resource. Rate quotas specify a time period, and the amount of the resource that you are permitted to consume over that time period.
